newsitem.title: UK: Rising demand in 1997 to lift most metals - Brandeis.
newsitem.headline: Rising demand in 1997 to lift most metals - Brandeis.

text.p: A pick-up in demand for industrial metals next year should lay the platform for rising prices for all markets except copper, according to brokers Brandeis in its 1997 Base Metals Outlook.
Demand in 1996 was depressed by a de-stocking phase, but re-stocking next year should help underpin the recovery.
--ALUMINIUM - Western world demand for aluminium is set to rise 3.5 percent in 1997 to 18.1 million tonnes following a year of almost no growth in 1996, Brandeis said.
But supply is set to exceed demand in 1997 and 1998 following a supply surplus in 1996, it added.
The surplus next year is likely to be 130,000 tonnes, compared with the 1996 level of 375,000 tonnes. In 1998 it could be much larger at 505,000 tonnes, Brandeis forecast.
As a result prices are likely to remain fairly flat over the next two years, with the 1997 average pegged at $1,575 a tonne on a three-month price basis from $1,550 in 1996.
--COPPER - Rising copper production is likely to depress values over the next two years, with three month futures forecast to slump to an average of $1,850 next year against $2,300 in 1996.
With stocks still at a low level of around 4.6 weeks' consumption, the market should remain in a $1,800 to $2,000 range for the remainder of the year, Brandeis said.
The report forecast a small supply surplus of 15,000 tonnes in 1996, rising to 240,000 tonne in 1997 and 445,000 tonnes in 1998.
--LEAD - The lead market is heading for a deficit of 63,000 tonnes in 1997 following a 92,000-tonne supply shortfall in 1996, Brandeis said.
Prices are forecast to increase to $830 next year from $800 in 1996.
--NICKEL - A rebound in consumption driven by higher stainless steel production is expected to help lift nickel values to an average of $8,598 in 1997 from $7,826 in 1996, Brandeis said.
Western demand is forecast to rise 4.1 percent to 908,000 tonnes next year after contracting two percent this year to 872,000 tonnes, it said.

The market is heading for a modest deficit of 6,000 tonnes next year after a 3,000-tonne shortfall in 1996. Sharply rising output in 1998 should return the market to a 4,000-tonne surplus, the report said.
Brandeis said CIS nickel output should remain stable at around 200,000 tonnes over the next few years.
--TIN - Prices are set to rise to $6,420 in 1997 from $6,285 in 1996 as stocks continue to be drawn down to seven weeks' consumption by the end of 1997.
--ZINC - "For the third year in a row the market will...record a deficit," Brandeis said.

The shortfall next year is expected to be 199,000 tonnes from 210,000 tonnes in 1996. A deficit of 164,000 tonnes is expected in 1998. This should bring down zinc stocks to 4.2 weeks' consumption by the end of 1998.
